hero.name: Thomas
hero.who: an accounts officer in Kochi who stopped drawing years ago and quietly misses it

story.b: Thomas used to draw comics in the back of his school notebooks, little stories about a lazy cat who ran a tea shop. His friends passed them around the class. Then came commerce, then coaching classes, then a job in the accounts department of a shipping firm in Ernakulam. Now he is thirty-six, good with spreadsheets, and the sketchbook his wife Anu gave him two birthdays ago is still under the bed, unopened. Some evenings he picks up a pen, stares at the blank page and feels his chest tighten. Who is he to draw now? He puts it back and watches cricket instead. But he misses the cat.

ask.q: Thomas wants to draw again but freezes in front of a blank page. What is a kind first step?
o: Wait until a great idea arrives and he feels ready
Sign up for an expensive art course to force himself
Start a small daily practice where nothing has to be good
ask.why: The blank page frightens him because he expects it to be good. A small daily practice with no pressure lets him show up without judging. Waiting to feel ready can stretch on forever, and an expensive course adds pressure and guilt to a creative self that needs gentle care.

chapters.take: Creativity returns through small, gentle practice, not by waiting to feel ready.

story.b: Thomas starts writing three pages by hand every morning before the ferry to work. No drawing, no plan, just whatever comes out. Day one is mostly complaints: the humidity, a vendor who has not sent an invoice, his knee. On day four he writes about the cat from school for half a page and is surprised. On day nine he writes the same money worry three times and finally sees it clearly. Nothing he writes is good, and nobody reads it, not even Anu. He keeps the notebook in his bag next to his lunch box. By the end of the month, his head feels less crowded on the ferry.

ask.q: After a week, Thomas rereads his morning pages and finds them boring and messy. What should he do?
o: Keep writing anyway, since the pages are for clearing his mind, not for reading
Stop, because messy writing is a waste of a morning
Edit them neatly so they become proper essays
ask.why: Morning pages are meant to empty out the clutter, not to be good writing. Boring and messy means they are working. Stopping throws away the clearing before it has a chance to help, and editing turns a free practice into another task with a critic watching.

chapters.take: Morning pages are not art. They clear space so art can come.

story.b: Thomas adds one more thing: a solo outing each week, just for curiosity. Anu raises an eyebrow but agrees to handle the Saturday shopping. The first Saturday, he takes the ferry to Fort Kochi with no plan. He wanders lanes he has never walked, watches an old man repair umbrellas, studies the peeling blue doors of old warehouses, and buys a small bottle of ink from a stationery shop that smells of paper. He does not draw anything. He just looks. That night, for the first time in years, a comic panel appears in his head on its own. A cat, mending umbrellas, under a sign in Malayalam.

ask.q: Thomas's friend Arun offers to join the weekly outing to make it more fun. What should Thomas do?
o: Agree, since company makes any outing better
Keep this outing solo, and plan a separate one with Arun
Skip the outings and use the time to draw instead
ask.why: The solo outing works because there is nobody to chat with or please, so his attention goes fully to what he sees. Bringing Arun turns it into a social trip. Skipping it to draw seems efficient, but it cuts off the fresh images his creativity needs.

chapters.take: Feed your imagination with regular solo outings just for curiosity.

story.b: On Sunday, Thomas finally opens the sketchbook and draws the umbrella cat. Within a minute, a familiar voice starts. The paws look wrong. You are thirty-six. Real artists went to art school. This is childish. Thomas almost closes the book. Then he tries something different. He writes the voice's words on a sticky note, and next to them he writes back. The paws can improve. Thirty-six is not old. This is just for me. He sticks the note on the wall and keeps drawing. The voice does not disappear. But it gets a little quieter by the end of the page, and the cat gets a little better.

ask.q: Anu wants to start singing again, but an inner voice tells her she is too old. What should Thomas suggest?
o: Wait until the critical voice goes quiet before she starts
Agree that it may be too late, to save her from disappointment
Treat the voice as noise, answer it back, and sing anyway
ask.why: The inner critic is noise, not truth, and it only quietens with practice. Answering it and singing anyway is how that practice happens. Waiting for silence means waiting forever, because the voice speaks loudest before we begin. Agreeing with it lets the critic win without a contest.

chapters.take: Your inner critic is noise, not truth. Keep making things anyway.

story.h: The page he runs for others
story.b: For six years, Thomas has run a small online page sharing comics by young artists from Kerala. He writes thoughtful reviews, knows every new name, and spends hours on it every week. People thank him for supporting the scene. One evening, while praising a student's work, he feels a strange ache. He has been standing right next to the thing he loves, helping everyone else do it, and never doing it himself. It is not that he lacks talent. He has been hiding. So he takes a small step. Without any big announcement, he posts one four-panel strip of the umbrella cat, alongside the others.

ask.q: Arun writes long reviews of every new film but has never tried writing a script. What gentle step would Thomas suggest?
o: Write even more reviews, since he is clearly a critic and not a creator
Try writing one short scene this week, just for himself
Quit reviewing completely until he finishes a full film script
ask.why: Staying close to an art you love without making it is often a sign of being blocked, not untalented. One small scene is a gentle first step. Calling himself only a critic closes the door, and demanding a full script at once is so big that it keeps him frozen.

chapters.take: Living beside the art you love may mean you are blocked, not untalented.

story.b: Thomas blocks two hours every Saturday morning, seven to nine, for drawing. He tells Anu, and she guards it like a shared secret. In the second week, his manager asks if he could come in on Saturday for a small task that could easily wait until Monday. In the third, a cousin wants help shifting furniture at eight. Thomas finds it hard to say no. But he treats the time as he would a promise to anyone else, and keeps showing up at the desk. Then small surprises start to arrive. A cafe near Marine Drive asks to display a few of his strips. A school teacher writes to ask if he would draw for their magazine.

ask.q: Thomas's manager asks him to give up his Saturday drawing time for a task that could wait. What should he do?
o: Politely protect the time and offer to handle the task first thing Monday
Give up the time, since creative hobbies matter less than work
Agree this once, and quietly resent it
ask.why: Treating creative time as a real commitment means protecting it like any other promise, especially from tasks that can wait. Offering Monday shows he still takes his work seriously. Giving it up teaches him creativity always comes last, and quiet resentment harms both the work and his peace.

chapters.take: Protect your creative time as seriously as any other commitment.

story.h: A cat in the cafe window
story.b: By the end of the year, Thomas has filled two sketchbooks. Most pages are rough. Some are good. He still writes three pages every morning before the ferry, and still takes a solo outing most Saturdays, often with his ink bottle now. The inner critic still talks, but he writes back faster. His comics page now shares his own strip every Friday alongside the young artists, and a few readers ask about the umbrella cat by name. Four of his strips hang in the cafe near Marine Drive. Anu has started music lessons on Thursday evenings. Sometimes, on the ferry, Thomas catches himself sketching the sky.

chapters.take: Creativity comes back when you show up for it gently and often.
